data.title: What operational data should never do
data.excerpt: Plant data becomes risky when it is copied without context, exposed without purpose, or trusted without lineage. Three boundaries worth designing early.
data.body:
Operational data is not generic business data. It describes physical processes, safety conditions, and the people running them. Treating it like web analytics creates both security and decision risk.

Boundary one: context travels with the value

A temperature of 84 means nothing without the asset, unit, timestamp, and quality flag. When data is copied into a warehouse without that context, every downstream team rebuilds its own interpretation.

Boundary two: exposure follows purpose

Not every analyst needs raw process values. Aggregate and derived data should be the default; raw streams should be an explicit, logged exception with a retention limit.

Boundary three: control networks stay controlled

Data collection should never create an inbound path into the control network. One-way gateways, allow-listed brokers, and documented change control are not optional.

  • Define a canonical asset and event model before integration.

  • Separate raw, curated, and published layers with different access.

  • Log every export of personally identifiable or safety-relevant data.

  • Test the recovery path, not only the happy path.

These boundaries cost less to design at the start than to retrofit after the first incident or the first contradictory board report.
